poiCHI-desc:
For more than a century China was the hegemon of the East, rising as its rivals were weakened by decades of social, political and economic upheaval. When the Great Mistake came, {{poiCHI001|the Chinese People's Party}} was the one government on Earth that had seen it coming. It had prepared its cities, its granaries and its coastlines long before the first warning, and for a time that foresight made China the sole world leader, taking the place the old United States had left empty.

The victory did not last. Decades of floods and environmental disasters have left Beijing barely able to hold {{poiCHI002|its own country}} together, let alone a sphere of influence that shrinks every year. Recovery came at a price: vast inequality, automation that has made millions redundant, and {{poiCHI003|corruption}} that reaches into every ministry. The result is a disenfranchised population that is growing more radical with each passing season.

The Cooperative is the successor to China's old sphere. Its members include Korea, {{poiCHI011|Japan}}, the mainland states of {{poiCHI010|Southeast Asia}} and the provinces of the Chinese People's Republic itself, tied together by {{poiCHI005|trade, shared defence}} and the memory of a stronger Beijing. Its provinces, from Guangdong and the Yangtze to Sichuan, {{poiCHI009|Dongbei}} and the Beijing region, are some of the richest and {{poiCHI004|most industrial places}} on Earth, and some of the most restless.

{{poiCHI006|The world's centre}} cannot hold.
poiCHI001-desc: China has been ruled by a single party since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949. Many reforms have come and gone since then, but in many ways the Chinese government is a relic of the world before the Great Mistake, poorly adapted to face the crisis now at its door.
poiCHI002-desc: After the Great Mistake, China emerged as the sole world leader, replacing the old United States. Decades of floods and other environmental disasters have since left it barely able to maintain control over its own territory, let alone a sphere of influence that keeps shrinking.
poiCHI003-desc: The death of Party Chairwoman Fu Zhong last year under suspicious circumstances has inflamed an already delicate political situation. National leadership is being contested between several factions of the People's Party, which degrades its already low legitimacy even further. Political groups outside the Party continue to grow in power, and the country becomes more decentralised by the year.
poiCHI004-desc: China faces many challenges, but it remains the undisputed world leader in many industrial sectors. Its large, well-educated population is unmatched by any other nation.
poiCHI005-desc: The Strategic Cooperation Organisation was formed in the golden age of Chinese international power, mainly as a means for Beijing to trade with its sphere and influence it. Decades of flooding have left that influence far weaker, and the organisation has taken on a more balanced role as an economic and military alliance. With political turmoil in many of its member states, the SCO may soon be relegated to the history books.
poiCHI006-desc: Last year Fu Zhong, China's de jure leader and the figurehead of the federal clique, died of a stroke at the relatively young age of 62. Her death has become the focus of many conspiracy theories, since it came in the middle of a succession dispute between the federal clique and the unitary clique led by {{poiCHI007|Liang Xiaowen}}. {{poiCHI008|Sun Zongying}} has since taken her place as leader of the federal clique, and the crisis shows no sign of ending.
poiCHI007-desc:
Liang Xiaowen leads the unitary clique. He is the incumbent Party Secretary and Mayor of Beijing, has served in government for over four decades, and is the self-declared provisional chairman of the Central Committee.

Born into a long line of politicians, Liang followed his parents into the Communist Party of China at 21, after studying political science. He began in the Beijing Clique alongside them, but switched sides to support the coup of 2159, going as far as to purge his own father from the Party to prove his loyalty. The re-established civilian government noticed this "commitment". Liang became one of the founding members of the Chinese People's Party under Xue Zemin, rising to Vice Premier of the State Council and a seat on the Politburo.

A falling-out with Xue saw him demoted to a minor post in Inner Mongolia, which conveniently spared him the worst of the corruption scandals that followed. He used his apparent opposition to Xue to cast himself as the anti-corruption reformer the aging bureaucracy needed. The populism made him famous, but the purge of his own family had cost him many allies who no longer wished to be seen with him.

Fu Zhong's rise to power in 2192, and her radical push for democratic federalism, gave Liang the opponent he needed. He rallied much of the Party's old guard into a reactionary unitary clique, and the mass strikes, the growing instability and the Chengdu uprising only seemed to prove him right. In 2198 he made his move. Using a violent dispute over water between the Tibetan and Qinghai regional governments as justification, he declared himself provisional chairman of the Central Committee in Beijing while Fu Zhong was away on a political tour of Fujian. It was the largest political crisis since the dissolution of the old Communist Party, and it has not ended since.
poiCHI008-desc:
Sun Zongying is a relative newcomer to politics. A famous actress, she was derided when Fu Zhong brought her into government, and her appointment as Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs in 2194 caused outrage in a Party proud of its technocratic character. The discontent faded, partly because Sun performed her role adequately even under intense scrutiny, and partly because far larger crises soon arrived.

Sun returned to the spotlight as the face of the federalist campaign for regional autonomy. Party rivals dismissed her as a paid actor, a celebrity hired to make a policy they claimed would tear the People's Republic apart more palatable. The strategy worked surprisingly well, as the opinion polls of the period show. In debates she held her own against sceptics and seasoned politicians alike, and after a clip of her demolishing a pro-unitary journalist went viral, the question of her competence became a national joke.

When Fu Zhong died, Sun was the obvious successor. She was arguably better known than her predecessor, and with the unitary clique already on the move there was no time for infighting. Even among her supporters, though, there are doubts about her commitment to the movement, and fears that a cult of personality is forming around her.
poiCHI009-desc:
Liu Zhihao is a prominent purist politician from Dongbei and the head of the National Revitalisation Movement within the Chinese People's Party. Born in Harbin to a family of doctors, he practised medicine before turning to politics out of disdain for the Xue administration. A capable administrator, he rose through the Party and held several senior roles in the Dongbei administration, all while openly opposing Fu Zhong and her reforms.

Fu Zhong's death and the chaos that followed gave Liu his opening. He promises a return to the glory of the old People's Republic, and his reactionism plays on a nostalgia that remains strong among older generations and among nationalists who feel China has lost its way. Technically a unitarist himself, he presents his movement as a third way between the unitaries and the federalists, and accuses both of failing to face the crisis the nation is in.
poiCHI010-desc:
Daoming Sochua was born to a Chinese mother and a Cambodian father, and raised in the traditions of both. Tested at genius level as a young child, she moved quickly through the state schools for gifted children, outpaced her parents (both university professors in the sciences) and her bright siblings, and entered university in her early teens, determined to outdo her older peers.

By thirty she held four doctorates, in electrical engineering, nano-electronics, nuclear physics and bubble fusion. Her methods for extracting energy from sources thought exhausted, and from deep-sea and off-world resources, earned her international awards and a post at the Chinese Bureau of Scientific Revolution. There she came to despise what she called a corrupt, nepotistic administration. Introduced by fellow researcher Tao Huiqing, she joined the Chinese Workers Party in 2195, a controversial move for a researcher of her standing.

After the Chengdu uprising and its brutal suppression by the central government, she resigned from the Bureau in protest and moved to Chongqing with many fellow revolutionaries, where the Workers Party is strong enough to keep the People's Party from intervening directly. She now holds a senior seat on the Workers' standing committee, aligned with the Party's cooperative wing, and has become its de facto figurehead.
poiCHI011-desc:
Born into a struggling Tokyo family, Iwata Masahiro spent his youth running deliveries for local food plants and attending practical lectures in his spare time. Japan had not yet recovered from the Great Mistake, and he saw the destruction of environmental collapse first-hand. As a teenager, after watching the rising tide wash away a local park, he vowed to rise to power and repair his homeland.

Too poor and undereducated for higher schooling, he spent most of his twenties with reclamation teams, where he built a reputation as a talented and resourceful worker. A scholarship from the Kubo Michi National Fund let him earn a degree in mechanical engineering. Over the following decades he travelled the country with the Ayame Keiretsu, took control of it at 41, and suddenly found himself one of the richest men in Japan.

He entered politics as an Innovationist candidate, but a string of failures and scandals pushed him into the Supremacist NKP, on whose coattails he rose to office and eventually became Prime Minister. His government is known for rebuilding, for promoting mechanical augmentation and for a deep reverence for natural parks. He is at odds with his own party on some issues, such as his friendly dealings with the Harmonist Innovationists, but he is widely seen as a great rebuilder and the architect of modern Japan.
